methods.label: Bound the forward projection
methods.explanation:
A perpendicular projection lets us combine the two sailing distances while keeping only one unknown length. Let \(\theta\) be the ship's turning angle from its forward direction at \(B\), so \(45^\circ<\theta<60^\circ\). Drop a perpendicular from \(C\) to the line \(AB\), meeting it at \(H\). Because the turn is acute, \(H\) lies beyond \(B\).

Write \(x=BH\) and \(y=CH\), measured in miles. The Pythagorean theorem in the two right triangles gives
\[
x^2+y^2=20^2=400
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
AC^2&=(10+x)^2+y^2\\
&=100+20x+x^2+y^2\\
&=500+20x.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus we only need bounds on the forward projection \(x\).

In right triangle \(BHC\), the angle at \(C\) is \(90^\circ-\theta\), which lies between \(30^\circ\) and \(45^\circ\). By the definition of sine,
\[
x=20\sin(90^\circ-\theta).
\]
Sine increases between \(0^\circ\) and \(90^\circ\), so the special-angle values give
\[
20\sin30^\circ<x<20\sin45^\circ,
\qquad 10<x<10\sqrt2.
\]
Substitution into \(AC^2=500+20x\) yields
\[
700<AC^2<500+200\sqrt2<800.
\]
The last inequality follows from \(\sqrt2<3/2\), since \(2<9/4\). Therefore \(AC^2\) lies in \([700,800]\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
